title: Positional Hierarchy
shortDefinition: A priority map showing which positions increase control, reduce risk, and open submissions.
whyItMatters: Without hierarchy, practitioners attack at the wrong time and skip survival, escape, or pinning.
deepExplanation: Hierarchy is not just a scoring list; it is a way to read risk. In bad positions, the goal is survival and structure. From top or pins, the goal is stabilization before finishing.
beginnerView: Learn which positions are dangerous and which are safer.
advancedView: Use hierarchy to decide when to reset, chain, or accept risk for score or submission.

ifThenExamples.if: If you lose Positional Hierarchy during the exchange.
ifThenExamples.then: Stop accelerating, recover the nearest body structure, then continue the technique.
ifThenExamples.why: Modern no-gi punishes forceful continuation after structure is lost.

ifThenExamples.if: If the opponent correctly answers your first line.
ifThenExamples.then: Use Positional Hierarchy to switch to a safer branch instead of forcing the same line.
ifThenExamples.why: A good concept turns the opponent’s reaction into information for the next decision.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Positional Hierarchy is a single technical trick.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: Treat it as a decision rule that appears across many positions.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Understanding the concept automatically makes it work live.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: The concept needs body signals, short cues, and positional rolling.

trainingCues: Name Positional Hierarchy before adding force.
Find the body signal instead of guessing generally.
If structure is lost, reset one layer first.
Drill slowly, then test with progressive resistance.
